slides.headline: The structure
slides.body: The test has 250 items in eighteen sections.

rows: One letter. Closed book, no terminal
Write the output you expect, as literally as you can, and one sentence of mechanism. No terminal
Draw the commit graph with every ref and HEAD, or answer the questions about the graph shown. No terminal
A real transcript is shown. Explain what happened, line by line where it matters, and what you would do next. No terminal
A situation is described. Give at least two hypotheses, the read-only command that separates them, the root cause with its layer, the fix and the prevention
A generated repository and a task card. Work in the lab shell; a check.sh verifies the end state
Written response in the seven stages of the incident loop, ending with the four-part summary
Spoken to an examiner, or recorded. Two to three minutes per answer, no notes, no terminal

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Six, from the test file.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: One. Closed book, except in the practical labs, where git help <command> and the manual pages are allowed and the textbook is not.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Two. Where an item says "no terminal", a terminal is a failed item.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Three. In prediction items you write <id> where an abbreviated commit ID would appear.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Four. In debugging and incident items, a state-changing command given before the root cause is established loses half of the item's points, whatever follows.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Five. GitHub-side items are answered from what you know of the documented behavior.

slides.headline: The rules
slides.body: Six. The practical labs follow the generator protocol of the incident drills: run the generator, open the lab shell at the path it prints, work, then run the check from the course root.

slides.headline: Why rule four exists
slides.body: It's the first fact of Chapter 29 made into a marking scheme: most damage is done after the incident, by the first repair attempt.

slides.headline: Why rule four exists
slides.body: A fixed opening is what replaces confidence, and the study the textbook cites found that experienced users were strongly represented among those asking Git questions.

slides.headline: The sittings
slides.body: Six, in this order, on separate days.

slides.headline: The pass rule
slides.body: Three conditions, all required.

slides.headline: After a section below 70 percent
slides.body: That section is retaken alone, after the restudy that the answer key names for each item.

slides.body: The test file contains no answers.

In every debugging and incident item, a state-changing command given before the root cause is established loses half of the item's points, whatever follows. A brilliant fix, reached by the right instinct, after the wrong first move, is worth half.
